summary:
Caribbean Netherlands comprises Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Dutch national law on civil status, marriage and anti-discrimination extends to the islands, and the statutory framework operating in the European Netherlands applies here in the same form.

That protection covers visitors as well as residents. Travel-facing coverage of the region treats Bonaire as a destination where strict anti-discrimination statutes stand behind an equality-friendly welcome, and the island markets itself on that basis.

Same-sex unions have been registrable since 4 December 2012, when the Census Office in Saba recorded the Caribbean Netherlands' first: Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Neither man was resident on the island; both were visiting, which establishes a local record of performing same-sex unions for people who are only passing through.

Ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry. The official weddings page of Saba Tourism identifies the Court Room in the Administrative Building as the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony and documents registrar Julieta Woods as flexible with couples' wishes, alongside a full destination-wedding supply chain of caterers, florists and accommodation. No source in the current inventory addresses gender-marker rules on identity documents, entry screening practice, access to gender-affirming care, or facilities and harassment exposure for trans visitors specifically; the findings above rest on marriage and anti-discrimination provisions rather than trans-specific legal text.
tangentialFactors:
The protection framework in the Caribbean Netherlands is inherited from the Netherlands rather than drafted locally, so the islands carry European-style equality statutes in a Caribbean setting. That combination is what regional travel press picks up when it ranks Bonaire among the more equality-friendly destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America.

The 2012 Saba registration involved two foreign nationals with no residence on the island, an Aruban and a Venezuelan. Marriages performed here can therefore involve non-resident couples, including nationals of jurisdictions where such unions are not available.
localsOnly:
Civil ceremonies are handled by the island registry on Saba, with the Court Room in the Administrative Building used for straightforward registrations and a registered registrar empowered to vary the ceremony to the couple's wishes.

Dutch national anti-discrimination law binds employers, service providers and public authorities in the three municipalities in the same way it does in the European Netherlands, giving residents a domestic legal remedy as well as a constitutional basis for complaint.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the current inventory: whether the Netherlands' rules on amending gender markers on passports and identity cards apply unchanged to residents of Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, and whether Dutch travel documents reflecting a gender change are accepted without questioning at local entry points.

Unresolved: local availability and cost of gender-affirming healthcare, including whether hormone therapy can be prescribed or continued on-island or requires referral to the Netherlands. No sourced reporting on documented violence against trans visitors, on police handling of complaints, or on public facilities access for trans people was available for this pass.
